The Maine constitution used to guarantee the right to keep and bear arms "for the common defense." In 1986 the Maine Supreme Court upheld a gun violation by focusing on the "common defense" phrase. The legislature, in response, enacted a constitutional amendment deleting that language declaring "Every citizen has a right to keep and bear arms, and this right shall never be questioned." The amendment was approved by voters in November 1987. Now a county superior court justice has ruled that even a convicted felon may own guns based on the amendment's all-inclusive language. The Maine Attorney General has announced that he will appeal the decision.

Ben Johnson, the world-class sprinter knocked off track and field's pedestal after testing positive for steroids now says that it's wrong to cheat and bad for health. Johnson said, "I got caught in Seoul. I lost my gold medal". Some US Congressional Representatives are presenting legislation to make anabolic steroids a controlled substance similar to the designation given to cocaine and heroin. The legislators emphasized increasing abuse of steroids by athletes at all levels. Johnson told other athletes not to make the mistake that he did urging them "to come forward, to come clean."

World-class sprinter Ben Johnson got knocked off track and field's pedestal and lost his gold medal in Seoul after testing positive for muscle-building steroids. At a news conference Thursday, as legislation was introduced to classify anabolic steroids as a controlled substance, Johnson told reporters it's wrong for athletes to use them, that they're bad for your health and it's wrong to cheat. Johnson was invited to attend by Representatives Mel Levine, Henry Waxman and Benjamin Gilman, presenters of the legislation, who applauded Johnson's courage in attending. Johnson later took the microphone and urged other athletes not to make the same mistake he did.
